groups.title: Making and using H₂
groups.rule: Hydrocarbon or water gives H₂ at high T (steam reforming, then the shift); a metal that dissolves in acid or base gives H₂ at the bench; electrolysis splits water.
groups.hook: Steam + carbon → CO + H₂; shift CO with more steam; metals displace H₂.

groups.title: Hydrides: making them and what they do
groups.rule: Hydride H⁻ is a base and a reducing agent: it takes H⁺ (or D⁺) from water, and it hands H⁻ to a metal or boron/aluminium halide.
groups.hook: H⁻ + H⁺ → H₂ (or HD with D₂O); H⁻ swaps for Cl⁻ to make the hydride reagents.

groups.title: Group 1 in oxygen, and the oxides with water and CO₂
groups.rule: Bigger cation, bigger anion: Li gives the oxide, Na the peroxide, K (Rb, Cs) the superoxide. Peroxide and superoxide give H₂O₂ with water; superoxide also eats CO₂ and gives O₂.
groups.hook: Li oxide, Na peroxide, K superoxide: O²⁻, O₂²⁻, O₂⁻ as the cation grows.

groups.title: Group 1: nitrogen, hydrogen, acetylene, alkyl halides
groups.rule: Li is the odd one out (nitride with N₂, organolithiums). Every alkali metal reduces H₂ to MH and takes H⁺ from acetylene.
groups.hook: Only Li takes N₂ directly; all of them make MH and carbides.

groups.title: Making Na and NaOH by electrolysis
groups.rule: Molten salt: the metal ion is reduced. Aqueous salt: water is reduced first (H₂ and OH⁻), so NaOH, H₂ and Cl₂ come out.
groups.hook: No water → Na metal (Downs). Brine → NaOH + H₂ + Cl₂ (chlor-alkali).

groups.title: Group 2 and beryllium
groups.rule: Be–Sr burn to the oxide, Ba to the peroxide. Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ gives the carbonate, then the soluble hydrogencarbonate. Be(OH)₂ is amphoteric, like Al.
groups.hook: Ba is the peroxide exception; Be reacts with acid and base.

groups.title: Boron: BX₃ and diborane
groups.rule: BX₃ are made from the oxide with a fluoride source (and acid). Diborane comes from BF₃ + hydride. Both hydrolyse to boric acid; B₂H₆ also burns and gives H₂.
groups.hook: B₂O₃ + F source → BF₃; BF₃ + NaH → B₂H₆; both + H₂O → B(OH)₃.

groups.title: Silicon: silanes and halides
groups.rule: SiH₄ comes from SiCl₄ and a hydride; it is hydrolysed by base to silicate + H₂. Silicon halides hydrolyse to SiO₂ (SiF₄ also takes F⁻ to [SiF₆]²⁻). Si is purified through SiHCl₃.

groups.title: Nitrogen: Haber → Ostwald → hydrazine → azide
groups.rule: N₂ + H₂ → NH₃ (Haber). NH₃ is burned over Pt to NO, then NO₂ and HNO₃ (Ostwald). NH₃ + OCl⁻ gives hydrazine (Olin–Raschig); NaNH₂ + N₂O gives azide (Wislicenus).
groups.hook: NH₃ is the hub: oxidise for HNO₃, chlorinate for N₂H₄, sodamide for N₃⁻.

groups.title: Nitrogen oxides, nitric acid and aqua regia
groups.rule: Concentrated HNO₃ oxidises (non-metals go to their highest oxoacid; NO₂ is the nitrogen product). Aqua regia makes NOCl and Cl₂, which dissolve gold as [AuCl₄]⁻.
groups.hook: Conc. HNO₃ → NO₂; aqua regia = HNO₃ + 3 HCl → NOCl + Cl₂.

groups.title: Phosphorus
groups.rule: Phosphate rock + sand + coke gives P₄. P₄ with F₂ goes to PF₅, with limited Cl₂ to PCl₃, with limited O₂ to P₄O₆, with excess O₂ to P₄O₁₀. PCl₃ and P₄O₆ hydrolyse to H₃PO₃; P₄O₁₀ gives H₃PO₄ and dehydrates amides.
groups.hook: Limited oxidant → P(III); excess → P(V); water on P(III) gives H₃PO₃, on P(V) gives H₃PO₄.

groups.title: Hydrogen peroxide, sulfur and chlorine dioxide
groups.rule: BaO₂ + acid gives H₂O₂, which disproportionates. The contact process takes SO₂ to SO₃ (V₂O₅), absorbs it in H₂SO₄ and dilutes. ClO₂ is made by reducing chlorate with SO₂.
groups.hook: Contact: oxidise, absorb in acid (oleum), dilute.

groups.title: Halogens and noble gases
groups.rule: A halogen higher up the group oxidises a halide below it. I₂ + I⁻ gives I₃⁻. Fluorine drives interhalogens and xenon fluorides to high oxidation states; HF comes from fluorspar and acid.
groups.hook: Cl₂ beats Br⁻ and I⁻; excess F₂ and heat give the highest fluoride.

groups.title: Nuclear equations
groups.rule: Mass number A and atomic number Z each balance on both sides. n: A 1, Z 0. α: A 4, Z 2. β⁻: A 0, Z +1 (n → p + e⁻). The unknown is read off the periodic table from Z.
groups.hook: Balance the top numbers, balance the bottom numbers, look up the symbol.

patterns.title: Elements burnt in O₂
patterns.rule: A small cation gives the normal oxide, a big cation a peroxide or superoxide (Li₂O, Na₂O₂, KO₂; Mg gives MgO but Ba gives BaO₂). Non-metals give covalent oxides: P₄ stops at P₄O₆ when O₂ is limited and goes to P₄O₁₀ in excess; sulfur burns to SO₂, not SO₃.

patterns.title: Basic anions + water
patterns.rule: Each of these anions takes H⁺ from water and leaves hydroxide: H⁻ gives H₂, N³⁻ gives NH₃, O²⁻ just gives OH⁻, O₂²⁻ gives H₂O₂ (and O₂⁻ gives H₂O₂ with some O₂ released).

patterns.title: Reactive metals + water, alcohol or acid
patterns.rule: Group 1 and 2 metals push H₂ out of anything with an acidic H: water gives the hydroxide + H₂, an alcohol gives the alkoxide + H₂, an acid gives the salt + H₂.

patterns.title: Covalent halides + water
patterns.rule: Covalent p-block halides are hydrolysed to the oxo-acid or oxide plus HX: BCl₃ to B(OH)₃, SiCl₄ to SiO₂, PCl₃ to H₃PO₃. SiF₄ keeps the fluoride as [SiF₆]²⁻. SF₆ is the exception: hydrolysis is favourable but it does not happen (kinetically inert).

patterns.title: Covalent hydrides (B₂H₆, SiH₄)
patterns.rule: They burn in O₂ to the oxide + water and are hydrolysed (water for B₂H₆, base for SiH₄) to give H₂ and the oxo-product.

patterns.title: Fluorine: highest oxidation states
patterns.rule: F₂ drives the central atom to its highest fluoride, and bigger atoms take more F (ClF₅, IF₇). Compare Cl₂, which stops P at PCl₃ where F₂ goes to PF₅. Xenon is oxidised too.

patterns.title: Chlorine
patterns.rule: Metals give ionic chlorides (NaCl, MgCl₂); non-metals give covalent ones (SiCl₄, PCl₃). Cl₂ also oxidises Br⁻ and I⁻ (a halogen higher up the group beats a halide below it).

patterns.title: Nitrogen and hydrogen
patterns.rule: Every alkali metal and Ca give a salt-like hydride with H₂. With N₂ only Li of Group 1 reacts directly (Li₃N); Mg burns in N₂ to Mg₃N₂. Nitrides then give NH₃ with water.

patterns.title: Halide acceptors: how many F⁻ they take
patterns.rule: Be and B stop at four-coordinate ([BeF₄]²⁻, [BF₄]⁻); Si and Sn go to six ([SiF₆]²⁻, [SnCl₆]²⁻) because they have room to expand.

patterns.title: Group 2 hydroxides: Be is the odd one
patterns.rule: CaO and the other oxides add water to give a base; Be(OH)₂ is amphoteric and reacts with acid and with NaOH.

exceptions.ask: Each metal is burnt in excess O₂. One does not give the plain oxide. Which?
exceptions.why: Mg (like Be to Sr) burns to the oxide; Ba, the big cation, takes the peroxide ion and gives BaO₂.

exceptions.ask: Four of these reactions work for every alkali metal. One does not. Which?

then.q: What happens with Na or K instead of Li?
then.right: No reaction (only Li takes N₂ directly)

exceptions.why: Only Li takes N₂ directly (Li₃N). Every alkali metal gives MH with H₂, loses H⁺ from acetylene, reacts with water, Cl₂ and alcohols.

exceptions.ask: Each covalent halide is shaken with water. Which one gives no reaction at all?

then.q: What is the outcome, and why?
then.right: No reaction: favourable but kinetically inert
wrong: No reaction: the reaction is thermodynamically uphill

exceptions.why: BCl₃, SiCl₄ and PCl₃ are hydrolysed at once. SF₆ has ΔG° = −221 kJ mol⁻¹ but is kinetically inert, so nothing happens.

exceptions.ask: Each halide is hydrolysed. In which one is the halogen NOT released as simple HX?

then.q: Where does the fluorine end up?

exceptions.why: BCl₃ and PCl₃ give the oxo-acid and HCl. SiF₄ gives SiO₂ and the fluoride is taken up as [SiF₆]²⁻.

exceptions.ask: Each of these is added to water. Which gives a product the others do not?
exceptions.why: H⁻ gives H₂, O²⁻ gives OH⁻, N³⁻ gives NH₃ and O₂²⁻ gives H₂O₂. The superoxide gives H₂O₂ and also O₂.

exceptions.ask: Each halide takes up one more halide ion or HF. Which product ion has a different coordination number from the other two?
exceptions.why: B has no room to expand and stops at [BF₄]⁻; Si and Sn go to six-coordinate ([SiF₆]²⁻, [SnCl₆]²⁻).

reactions.name: Steam reforming
reactions.ask: Write steam reforming of methane (nickel catalyst, about 1200 K).
reactions.hook: Methane plus steam gives synthesis gas: CO and three H₂.
reactions.note: The hydrogen slides before slide 25 are not in the uploaded decks, so this is bank-only.

reactions.name: Water–gas shift
reactions.ask: Write the water–gas shift reaction (iron oxide catalyst, about 700 K).
reactions.hook: Shift the O from water onto CO: more H₂, CO₂ out.
reactions.note: Bank-only (hydrogen slides before slide 25 are not in the uploaded decks).

reactions.name: Coke and steam
reactions.ask: Write the reaction of coke with steam at 1000–1200 K.
reactions.hook: Hot carbon strips O from steam: CO + H₂ ("water gas").
reactions.note: Bank-only (hydrogen slides before slide 25 are not in the uploaded decks).

reactions.ask: Write the laboratory preparation of H₂ from zinc and dilute HCl.
reactions.hook: Metal above H in the series displaces H₂ from acid.
reactions.note: Bank-only: not in the uploaded decks.

reactions.ask: Write the laboratory preparation of H₂ from aluminium and aqueous NaOH.
reactions.hook: Amphoteric Al dissolves in base as the tetrahydroxoaluminate.
reactions.note: Bank-only: not in the uploaded decks.

reactions.ask: Electrolysis of water in acid: write the anode and cathode half-equations (one per line, with e⁻).
reactions.hook: Anode oxidises water (O₂ + H⁺); cathode reduces H⁺.

reactions.ask: Electrolysis of water in base: write the anode and cathode half-equations (one per line, with e⁻).
reactions.hook: Anode oxidises OH⁻; cathode reduces water to H₂ + OH⁻.

reactions.ask: Write the formation of HCl from H₂ and Cl₂ (a light-initiated radical chain).
reactions.cond: light starts the chain (Cl–Cl is the weak bond)
reactions.hook: Cl• takes H from H₂; H• takes Cl from Cl₂; the cycle repeats.

reactions.ask: Write the catalytic hydrogenation of carbon monoxide to methanol over ZnO.
reactions.hook: CO takes two H₂ to become CH₃OH.

reactions.ask: Write the reaction of CaH₂ with water (why it is a drying agent).
reactions.hook: H⁻ takes H⁺ from water: H₂ and hydroxide, so it removes water.

reactions.ask: Write NaH reacting with D₂O.
reactions.hook: H⁻ takes one D⁺: essentially pure HD.
reactions.note: From the bank (the HD question); the slides print no D₂O equation.

reactions.name: Lithium aluminium hydride synthesis
reactions.ask: Write the synthesis of lithium aluminium hydride from LiH and Al₂Cl₆.
reactions.hook: Hydride swaps for chloride; the Al ends up as AlH₄⁻.

reactions.name: Sodium borohydride synthesis
reactions.ask: Write the synthesis of sodium borohydride from NaH and BCl₃.
reactions.hook: Three H⁻ swap for Cl⁻; the fourth H⁻ binds B.

reactions.ask: Hydride is a strong reducing agent: write the reaction of TiCl₄ with LiH to give Ti metal.
reactions.hook: Four H⁻ give up their electrons, leaving H₂.

reactions.ask: Write the reaction of a Group 1 metal (sodium) with H₂.
reactions.hook: All alkali metals reduce H₂ to the saline hydride MH.

reactions.ask: Write lithium burning in oxygen.
reactions.hook: Li is small: the oxide O²⁻.

reactions.ask: Write sodium heated in oxygen (the principal product).
reactions.hook: Na: the peroxide O₂²⁻ (diamagnetic, singlet).

reactions.ask: Write potassium heated in oxygen (the principal product).
reactions.hook: K, Rb, Cs: the superoxide O₂⁻ (one unpaired electron).

reactions.ask: Write sodium peroxide with water.
reactions.hook: Peroxide + water → hydroxide + hydrogen peroxide.

reactions.ask: Write potassium superoxide with water.
reactions.hook: Superoxide + water → hydroxide + H₂O₂ and O₂.

reactions.ask: KO₂ absorbs CO₂ and releases O₂ (breathing apparatus, submarines). Write the equation (product: K₂CO₃).
reactions.hook: It swaps CO₂ out for O₂: a breathing-apparatus scrubber.
reactions.note: The slides say KO₂ absorbs CO₂ and releases O₂ but print no equation; K₂CO₃ as the product comes from the bank.

reactions.ask: Li is the only alkali metal that reacts directly with N₂. Write the equation.
reactions.hook: Only Li makes a nitride directly; Li₃N is a fast-ion conductor.

reactions.ask: Write the reaction of Li₃N with water (a lab source of NH₃).
reactions.hook: N³⁻ is a very strong base: it takes three H⁺.

reactions.ask: Write the reaction of sodium with acetylene.
reactions.hook: Acetylene is acidic enough to lose both H⁺: carbide + H₂.

reactions.ask: Write the formation of ethyllithium from Li metal and chloroethane.
reactions.hook: Two Li: one goes into C–Li, one makes LiCl.
reactions.note: The slides mention RLi reagents but print no preparation.

reactions.name: Downs cell
reactions.ask: Write the overall equation for electrolysis of molten NaCl (the Downs cell).
reactions.hook: No water: Na⁺ is reduced, Cl⁻ is oxidised.
reactions.note: The slides print 2NaCl → 2Na + Cl₂ (electrolysis of fused salts); "Downs cell" is the name from the bank.

reactions.name: Chlor-alkali process
reactions.ask: Write the overall equation for electrolysis of aqueous NaCl (chlor-alkali).
reactions.hook: Water is reduced before Na⁺: H₂ and OH⁻ at the cathode.
reactions.note: The slides print the equation; "chlor-alkali" is the name from the bank.

reactions.ask: Electrolysis of molten KBr: write the anode and cathode half-equations (one per line, with e⁻).
reactions.hook: Anode oxidises the anion, cathode reduces the cation.

reactions.ask: Write magnesium burning in oxygen (Be to Sr give the normal oxide).
reactions.hook: Be–Sr: oxide.

reactions.ask: Write the combustion of barium in O₂.
reactions.hook: Ba is the big cation, so it takes the peroxide.

reactions.ask: Write the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate.
reactions.hook: Small cations pull the carbonate apart at lower T.

reactions.ask: Bubbling CO₂ through limewater first gives a milky suspension, then a clear solution with more CO₂. Write both balanced equations (one per line).
reactions.hook: Milky = CaCO₃; excess CO₂ turns it into soluble Ca(HCO₃)₂.
reactions.note: The slides print only the first equation and say the solid "disappears on further reaction with CO₂" (soluble Ca(HCO₃)₂).

reactions.ask: Mg burns in N₂ to form a nitride, which reacts with water to give ammonia. Write both equations.
reactions.hook: Li and Mg are diagonal neighbours: both nitrides, both give NH₃ with water.

reactions.ask: Be(OH)₂ is amphoteric. Write its reaction with NaOH.
reactions.hook: Amphoteric like Al(OH)₃: dissolves in base to [Be(OH)₄]²⁻.

reactions.ask: Write the reaction of Be(OH)₂ with sulfuric acid.
reactions.hook: The same hydroxide also acts as a base.

reactions.ask: Write the synthesis of anhydrous BeCl₂ from BeO and CCl₄ (1070 K).
reactions.hook: Anhydrous: CCl₄ chlorinates BeO and takes the oxygen as CO₂.

reactions.ask: Write the reduction of B₂O₃ with magnesium to give amorphous boron.
reactions.hook: Mg takes the oxygen.

reactions.name: BF₃ from the oxide
reactions.ask: Write the laboratory synthesis of BF₃ from B₂O₃, CaF₂ and concentrated H₂SO₄.
reactions.hook: Acid + fluorspar make HF in situ; HF converts the oxide.

reactions.name: Diborane synthesis
reactions.ask: Write the industrial synthesis of B₂H₆ from BF₃ and NaH (450 K).
reactions.hook: H⁻ swaps for F⁻; the three-centre bonds form the dimer.

reactions.ask: Write the hydrolysis of diborane.
reactions.hook: Each B–H gives H₂; boric acid is left.

reactions.ask: Write the combustion of diborane.
reactions.hook: Burns to B₂O₃ and water.

reactions.ask: Write the hydrolysis of BCl₃.
reactions.hook: BX₃ is a Lewis acid: water attacks and chloride leaves.

reactions.ask: Write BCl₃ with liquid ammonia (aminolysis).
reactions.hook: Three NH₃ substitute, three more take the HCl as NH₄Cl.

reactions.ask: Write the formation of tetrafluoroboric acid from BF₃ and HF.
reactions.hook: BF₃ accepts F⁻ and becomes a strong acid.

reactions.ask: Write the synthesis of silane from SiCl₄ and LiAlH₄.
reactions.hook: Hydride and chloride trade places.

reactions.ask: Write the hydrolysis of SiH₄ by aqueous KOH (product: potassium silicate K₂SiO₃).
reactions.hook: Base cleaves every Si–H: four H₂.

reactions.name: Purification of silicon
reactions.ask: Write the formation of trichlorosilane from impure Si and anhydrous HCl (300 °C), the first step in purifying Si.
reactions.hook: Distil the volatile SiHCl₃, then decompose it to pure Si.

reactions.ask: Write the synthesis of trisilylamine from SiH₃Cl and NH₃.
reactions.hook: Three Si–Cl react; extra NH₃ takes the HCl.

reactions.ask: Write the reaction of SiH₃Cl with water vapour to give disilyl ether.
reactions.hook: Two SiH₃ share one O.

reactions.ask: Write the synthesis of SiF₄ from SiO₂, CaF₂ and concentrated H₂SO₄.
reactions.hook: The same trick as BF₃: acid + fluorspar.

reactions.ask: Write the hydrolysis of liquid SiCl₄.
reactions.hook: Si has empty d-type access: water attacks, silica forms.

reactions.ask: SiF₄ is a mild Lewis acid. Write SiF₄ accepting fluoride ions.
reactions.hook: Four-coordinate to six-coordinate.
reactions.note: The slides call SiF₄ a mild Lewis acid and show [SiF₆]²⁻; the equation is written out here.

reactions.name: Haber–Bosch process
reactions.ask: Write the Haber process equation.
reactions.cond: Fe₃O₄ catalyst, about 500 °C, 500 atm (the slides also quote 400 °C, 250 atm)
reactions.hook: Hub of the nitrogen chart: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃.

reactions.name: Ostwald process
reactions.ask: Write the equations for the Ostwald process from NH₃ to HNO₃ (Pt catalyst, about 1300 K for the first step).
reactions.hook: Burn NH₃ to NO, oxidise to NO₂, dissolve in water (NO is recycled).
reactions.note: The slides print only step 1 (Pt, 1300 K). Steps 2 and 3 come from the bank.

reactions.name: Olin–Raschig process
reactions.ask: Write the Olin–Raschig process (overall, or as its two steps via chloramine).
alt: NH2Cl + NH3 + NaOH -> N2H4 + NaCl + H2O
reactions.hook: Hypochlorite makes chloramine, which couples with a second NH₃.
reactions.note: The slides print the overall equation and mention chloramine; the two-step route is that path.

reactions.name: Wislicenus process
reactions.ask: With chemical equations, explain the Wislicenus process (two steps).
reactions.hook: Sodium makes sodamide; sodamide plus N₂O gives sodium azide.

reactions.ask: Write the decomposition of sodium azide in an airbag.
reactions.hook: Azide decomposes to N₂ gas, which inflates the bag.

reactions.ask: TNT (C₇H₅N₃O₆) decomposes to N₂, H₂O, CO and soot (C). Write the balanced equation.
reactions.hook: Oxygen-poor explosive: lots of CO and carbon.

reactions.ask: Write the laboratory preparation of NH₃ by heating NH₄Cl with Ca(OH)₂.
reactions.hook: A base frees NH₃ from its ammonium salt.

reactions.ask: Ammonia cleaners and hypochlorite bleach must never be mixed. Write the reaction of NH₃ with OCl⁻ that forms the toxic gas.
reactions.hook: The first step of Olin–Raschig: chloramine.
reactions.note: The slides say chloramine forms but print no equation.

reactions.ask: Write the neutralisation that makes the fertiliser NH₄NO₃ from NH₃ and nitric acid.
reactions.hook: Base + acid; the nitrogen chart ends in ammonium nitrate.
reactions.note: The slides show NH₃ + HX → NH₄X; the nitrate case is the end of the nitrogen chart.

reactions.ask: Write the preparation of N₂O (laughing gas) by careful heating of ammonium nitrate (250 °C).
reactions.hook: Internal redox of NH₄⁺ and NO₃⁻.

reactions.ask: Write the preparation of NO₂ from copper and concentrated nitric acid.
reactions.hook: Concentrated acid gives NO₂ (dilute would give NO).

reactions.ask: N₂O₅ is the anhydride of nitric acid. Write its preparation by dehydrating HNO₃ with P₂O₅ (product also H₃PO₄).
reactions.hook: P₂O₅ is the dehydrating agent.

reactions.ask: NO₂/N₂O₄ are corrosive because they react with water. Write (i) N₂O₄ + H₂O and (ii) the disproportionation of HNO₂.
reactions.hook: Mixed anhydride: HNO₃ + HNO₂, and HNO₂ disproportionates.

reactions.ask: Concentrated HNO₃ oxidises I₂ to HIO₃ and is itself reduced to NO₂. Write the balanced equation.
reactions.hook: Conc. HNO₃ takes a non-metal to its highest oxoacid.
reactions.note: The slides name the products (HIO₃, H₃PO₄, H₂SO₄) but print no equations.

reactions.ask: Concentrated HNO₃ oxidises P₄ to H₃PO₄ (NO₂ formed). Write the balanced equation.
reactions.hook: Every P goes to +5, five NO₂ each.
reactions.note: The slides name the products (HIO₃, H₃PO₄, H₂SO₄) but print no equations.

reactions.ask: Concentrated HNO₃ oxidises S₈ to H₂SO₄ (NO₂ formed). Write the balanced equation.
reactions.hook: Every S goes to +6: six NO₂ each.
reactions.note: The slides name the products (HIO₃, H₃PO₄, H₂SO₄) but print no equations.

reactions.name: Aqua regia
reactions.ask: Aqua regia (1:3 conc. HNO₃ : HCl) dissolves Au(0) to give HAuCl₄. Write the balanced equation(s).
steps: Au + NOCl + Cl2 + HCl -> HAuCl4 + NO
reactions.hook: HNO₃ oxidises; Cl⁻ complexes Au³⁺ as [AuCl₄]⁻, which pulls the reaction over.
reactions.note: The slide prints H₂O (not 2H₂O) in the first step; 2H₂O is what balances.

reactions.ask: Balance: NaClO₃ + SO₂ + H₂SO₄ → ClO₂ + NaHSO₄ (write the balanced equation).
reactions.hook: SO₂ reduces Cl(V) to Cl(IV): yellow-green odd-electron ClO₂.

reactions.name: White phosphorus from phosphate rock
reactions.ask: Write the extraction of white phosphorus from phosphate rock, sand and coke.
reactions.cond: about 1700 K, sand and coke; the P₄ vapour is condensed under water
reactions.hook: Coke reduces P(V); sand takes the calcium as CaSiO₃.

reactions.ask: White phosphorus is treated with fluorine gas. Write the equation.
reactions.hook: Excess F₂ takes P to +5; PF₅ is trigonal bipyramidal, a Lewis acid.

reactions.ask: Write the formation of PCl₃ from white phosphorus.
reactions.hook: Limited oxidant gives P(III).

reactions.ask: Write the formation of PF₃ from CaF₂ and PCl₃ (driven by the stronger P–F bond).
reactions.hook: P–F (490) beats P–Cl (322 kJ mol⁻¹).

reactions.ask: Write the hydrolysis of PCl₃.
reactions.hook: P(III) stays P(III): phosphorous acid, not phosphoric.

reactions.ask: Write the controlled oxidation of P₄ to P₄O₆ (an O inserted into each P–P bond).
reactions.hook: Six P–P edges, six bridging O.

reactions.ask: Write the further oxidation of P₄O₆ to P₄O₁₀.
reactions.hook: Four terminal O added, one per P.
reactions.note: The slides describe it (terminal O added to each P) but print no equation.

reactions.ask: Write P₄O₆ with water.
reactions.hook: P(III) oxide gives phosphorous acid.

reactions.ask: Write P₄O₁₀ with water.
reactions.hook: P(V) oxide gives phosphoric acid.

reactions.ask: P₄O₁₀ is a powerful dehydrating agent. Write the dehydration of benzamide (PhCONH₂) to benzonitrile (PhCN), with H₃PO₄ as the other product.
reactions.hook: It removes H₂O from –CONH₂ to leave –C≡N (balanced from the scheme in the notes).
reactions.note: The slide shows RCONH₂ → RCN with P₄O₁₀ and −H₂O; the balanced equation is worked out here.

reactions.name: Wet method for phosphoric acid
reactions.ask: Write the manufacture of H₃PO₄ from phosphate rock and sulfuric acid (the "wet method").
reactions.hook: A stronger acid displaces the weaker; CaSO₄ precipitates.

reactions.ask: Write phosphoric acid with one equivalent of NH₃ (the first step to ammonium phosphate fertilisers).
reactions.hook: Neutralise one acidic H.

reactions.name: Thenard preparation
reactions.ask: Write Thenard's preparation of H₂O₂ from barium peroxide and dilute H₂SO₄.
reactions.hook: BaSO₄ precipitates, leaving H₂O₂.

reactions.ask: Write the disproportionation of hydrogen peroxide (oxidation numbers −1 to −2 and 0).
reactions.hook: The same O goes both down (to water) and up (to O₂).
reactions.note: The slides write H₂O₂ → H₂O + ½O₂ (ΔH° = −98 kJ mol⁻¹); doubled here.

reactions.name: Contact process
reactions.ask: Write the three steps that turn SO₂ into sulfuric acid in the contact process (oxidation; absorption into acid; dilution).
reactions.hook: Oxidise, absorb in acid to make oleum (H₂S₂O₇), dilute.
reactions.note: The slides write SO₂ + ½O₂ → SO₃ (V₂O₅); the doubled form is the same reaction.

reactions.ask: Write the hydrolysis of SF₆ (thermodynamically favourable, ΔG° = −221 kJ mol⁻¹, yet it does not happen).
reactions.hook: Kinetically inert, not thermodynamically: no low-energy pathway.

reactions.ask: Write chlorine bubbled into aqueous bromide.
reactions.hook: The halogen higher up the group wins.
reactions.note: The slides give the rule (a halogen higher up oxidises a halide below it) but no equation.

reactions.ask: Write chlorine bubbled into aqueous iodide.
reactions.hook: Same rule: Cl₂ oxidises I⁻.
reactions.note: The slides give the rule but no equation.

reactions.ask: I₂ dissolves readily in aqueous KI. Write the equation.
reactions.hook: I⁻ donates into the σ* of I₂: linear I₃⁻.

reactions.ask: Write the reaction of I₂ with F₂ at room temperature (the interhalogen with five F).
reactions.hook: Room temperature stops at IF₅.
reactions.note: Text only on the slides (IF₅ at room temperature).

reactions.ask: Write the reaction of I₂ with F₂ at 250–300 °C (the interhalogen with seven F).
reactions.hook: More heat and excess F₂ reach IF₇.
reactions.note: Text only on the slides (IF₇ at 250–300 °C).

reactions.ask: Write the production of HF from fluorspar (CaF₂) and concentrated H₂SO₄.
reactions.hook: A strong non-volatile acid displaces volatile HF.

reactions.ask: Write xenon reacting with fluorine to give the +2 fluoride.
reactions.hook: Linear XeF₂.

reactions.ask: Write xenon reacting with excess fluorine at 400 °C (the +4 fluoride).
reactions.hook: Square-planar XeF₄.

reactions.ask: Capture of an α-particle (⁴He) by ²²Ne, followed by release of a neutron, gives species X. Which isotope of which element is X?
²³⁸U captures a neutron, then undergoes two successive β⁻ decays. What isotope results?
reactions.hook: A: 238 + 1 = 239. Each β⁻ adds 1 to Z: 92 → 93 → 94, plutonium.

reactions.ask: Natural tritium forms by neutron capture by nitrogen: ¹⁴N + n → T + X. What is X?
⁹Be + ⁴He → n + X. What is X?
reactions.hook: A: 9 + 4 = 1 + 12. Z: 4 + 2 = 0 + 6, carbon-12 (the discovery of the neutron).

reactions.ask: Write the formation of HF from H₂ and F₂ (at −196 °C).
reactions.cond: works at −196 °C: F₂ is that reactive
reactions.hook: The most reactive halogen needs no heat to take H₂.

reactions.ask: Write the burning of hydrogen in oxygen (a radical chain; mixtures explode).
reactions.hook: The strong O–H bond (464 kJ mol⁻¹) drives it.

reactions.ask: Write sodium with water at room temperature.
reactions.hook: Water is reduced to H₂ and OH⁻; vigour rises from Li to Cs.

reactions.ask: Write lithium oxide with water.
reactions.hook: Oxide, peroxide and superoxide all give the hydroxide.

reactions.ask: Write sodium with chlorine.
reactions.hook: Group 1 metals reduce every halogen.

reactions.ask: Write sodium with ethanol (an alkoxide forms).
reactions.hook: M + ROH → MOR + ½H₂: the same H⁺ reduction as with water.

reactions.ask: Write CaO with water (Ca, Sr and Ba oxides; Be and Mg oxides are stable).
reactions.hook: Basic oxide plus water gives the hydroxide, exothermically.

reactions.ask: Write magnesium with hot water.
reactions.cond: heating required (Mg is passivated); Be does not react
reactions.hook: Ca, Sr and Ba react the same way, more readily.

reactions.ask: Write magnesium dissolving in dilute HCl.
reactions.hook: Be and Mg dissolve readily in dilute acids with H₂.

reactions.ask: Write calcium with H₂ under high pressure.
reactions.hook: Be is the exception: it does not react with H₂.

reactions.ask: Write the saline hydride CaH₂ with water in the general form MH₂ + 2H₂O (take M = Ca).
reactions.hook: The same drying-agent reaction as in the hydrides chunk.

reactions.ask: Write magnesium with chlorine.
reactions.hook: Direct combination with X₂ gives the ionic halides.

reactions.ask: Write Ca₃N₂ with H₂ (gives CaNH and CaH₂).
reactions.hook: The nitride is hydrogenated rather than hydrolysed.
reactions.note: The slide prints 2CaH₂, which leaves Ca unbalanced (4 against 3); one CaH₂ balances.

reactions.ask: Write the reaction of calcium carbonate with carbon (calcium carbide forms).
reactions.hook: Marked with an asterisk on the slide: a side note, low priority.

reactions.ask: Write BeF₂ with sodium fluoride (BeF₂ is a Lewis acid).
reactions.hook: Be²⁺ takes two F⁻ to reach four-coordinate [BeF₄]²⁻.

reactions.ask: Write BeCl₂ dissolving in water (it forms the aqua ion).
reactions.hook: Small, highly charged Be²⁺ makes the acidic [Be(H₂O)₄]²⁺.
reactions.note: The slide prints the product as [Be(H₂O)₄]₂X, a typo for [Be(H₂O)₄]X₂.

reactions.ask: Write the reduction of BCl₃ with zinc to give boron.
reactions.hook: Zn takes the chlorine; the other route uses Mg and B₂O₃.

reactions.ask: Write the synthesis of BCl₃ from B₂O₃, carbon and chlorine.
reactions.hook: Carbon strips the oxygen as CO while Cl₂ replaces it.

reactions.ask: Write the Lewis adduct of BF₃ with methanol.
reactions.hook: BF₃ is a Lewis acid: the planar sp² boron becomes tetrahedral.

reactions.ask: Write Al₂O₃ with HF to make AlF₃ (970 K).
reactions.hook: HF swaps fluoride for oxide.

reactions.ask: Write aluminium with fluorine (the general 2M + 3F₂ → 2MF₃).
reactions.hook: Direct combination gives the trifluoride.

reactions.ask: Write silane burning in air.
reactions.hook: Silane is explosively inflammable, unlike methane.

reactions.ask: Write the formation of SiH₃Cl from silane and HCl.
reactions.hook: One H swaps for Cl; the other route is Si + HCl.

reactions.ask: Write the carbon reduction of silica to silicon.
reactions.hook: Carbon removes the oxygen as CO.
reactions.note: The slide prints CO₂ on the right, which does not balance; 2CO does.

reactions.ask: Write the formation of liquid SiCl₄ from silicon.
reactions.hook: Direct reaction with Cl₂.

reactions.ask: Write the hydrolysis of SiF₄ (fluorosilicic acid forms).
reactions.hook: Both SiF₄ and SiCl₄ hydrolyse; SiF₄ keeps some fluoride as [SiF₆]²⁻.

reactions.ask: Write SnCl₄ with potassium chloride (tin(IV) halides are strong Lewis acids).
reactions.hook: Tin(IV) halides resemble the Si and Ge ones and add halide.

reactions.ask: Write the preparation of nitrous acid from barium nitrite and sulfuric acid.
reactions.hook: A mineral acid frees the weak acid; BaSO₄ precipitates.
reactions.note: The slide prints barium nitrite as Ba(NO)₂, a typo.

reactions.ask: Write hydrazine burning in oxygen (rocket fuel).
reactions.hook: Strongly exothermic: N₂ and water.

reactions.ask: Write NO reacting with oxygen in air.
reactions.hook: Immediate: this makes NO₂ in polluted air.

reactions.ask: Write the formation of N₂O₃ from NO and NO₂ (below −101 °C).
reactions.hook: It dissociates again as it warms.
reactions.note: The bank uses this step; the slide shows N₂O₃ ⇌ NO + NO₂.

reactions.ask: Write phosphoric acid with two equivalents of NH₃.
reactions.hook: Two acidic H atoms neutralised: the diammonium phosphate fertiliser.

reactions.ask: Write sulfur burning in oxygen.
reactions.hook: S₈ ring to eight SO₂.

reactions.ask: Write SO₃ with water (a strongly acidic oxide).
reactions.hook: In the contact process this is avoided: water gives a mist, so SO₃ is absorbed in H₂SO₄ instead.

reactions.ask: Write the other route to ClO₂: sodium chlorate reduced by hydrochloric acid.
reactions.hook: Cl(V) goes to Cl(IV); the HCl gives Cl₂ and NaCl.

reactions.ask: Write Cl₂ with F₂ at 225 °C (the lowest interhalogen).
reactions.hook: Raise F₂ and T to go up: ClF₃, then ClF₅.

reactions.ask: Write Cl₂ with excess F₂ at 300 °C.
reactions.hook: Odd numbers of F only: XX′ₙ with n odd.

reactions.ask: Write Cl₂ with F₂ at 350 °C and 250 atm.
reactions.hook: High F₂ pressure is what reaches the pentafluoride.
